items.description:

Market liberalization has dropped the cost of internet to $65.00 per Mbps per month to just 78 cents, while more than 1,500 kilometers of undersea fiber optic cables […] The post Internet Access Soars, Costs Plummet on Island Following the End its Federal Telecom Monopoly appeared first on Good News Network .
global_silver_linings.reason: When monopolies are broken up, real people benefit — faster, cheaper internet reaching an island community is a quiet but powerful reminder that structural change can genuinely improve everyday life. It's proof that better access to the wider world doesn't have to be a privilege.

discovery_articles.title: The Living History Museum of Camping in Phelps, Wisconsin
discovery_articles.snippet: In Wisconsin's Northwoods, nobody ever went "to the cabin" — they went to the camp , whether that meant a canvas tent, a camper, or the family cottage on the lake. A resort on North Twin Lake has turned that whole tradition into America's first living history museum of camping — a museum where the exhibits have beds, and guests are encouraged to sleep in them. The collection spans a century, one decade per unit: two Prohibition-era luxury tents named for Al Capone and John Dillinger, who genuinely vacationed (and hid) in these woods — Dillinger's famous FBI shootout happened one lake chain over.

discovery_articles.title: Schwarzer Turm in Mödling, Austria
discovery_articles.snippet: This (more gray than) "black tower" is part of a whole series of picturesque viewpoints constructed in and around the small town Mödling commissioned by Johann I., Prince of Liechtenstein. It was built in 1809 and 1810 according to the plans of the architect Joseph Hardtmuth. It was most likely originally intended as an observation tower and was later also used as a forester’s residence.

featured_read.title: The Bird in You, the World in You, and the Art of Trusting Time: A Ceramics and Serpentine Raffle
featured_read.snippet: One December afternoon, I arrived in Patagonia with a big blue backpack, a small bilingual edition of Pablo Neruda’s love poems, and a broken heart. (Though a heart, of course, never breaks.) The moment I stepped out of the airplane, the Andes towered over me like the stone thrones of gods, snow-capped over the oracle eye of the glacial lake, blue as Uranus, their scale so incomprehensible you are no longer a person but a particle, a mote of dust in the eye of eternity; the trees are no longer trees but moss carpeting the slopes all the way down… read article
featured_read.blurb: This essay asks what happens to grief when you carry it somewhere vast enough to dwarf it — arriving in Patagonia with a broken heart and Neruda, the writer discovers that scale itself can be a kind of medicine. Set aside the half-hour for the moment the Andes turn a person back into a particle, and what quietly grows in that reduction.
